title: Public Defender’s Office legislative priorities include more funding, more equitable sentencing
summary: The Maryland Office of the Public Defender laid out a legislative agenda Wednesday that calls for more funding for the office as well changes to sentencing and search laws, among others, that will help public defenders do their jobs.
content:
by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters January 21, 2026

by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters January 21, 2026

The Maryland Office of the Public Defender laid out a legislative agenda Wednesday that calls for more funding for the office as well changes to sentencing and search laws, among others, that will help public defenders to their jobs.

“We are tired, bone tired, of fighting a system that was designed to fail the very people that we represent,” Public Defender Natasha Dartigue during a chilly rally on Lawyers Mall.

Dartigue, joined by lawmakers and advocates, recalled the words of the late author and activist James Baldwin, who said, “Not everything that is faced can be changed, but nothing can be changed until it is faced.”

“So we’re here today to face it, to speak with truth and conviction as to what Marylanders need to know and hear, and what our dedicated representatives here in Annapolis need to do in the remaining 83 days of session,” she said.

That includes providing more resources for her office and passing  legislation to end the state’s practice of automatically charging youth as adults.

Dartigue is also calling for passage of Del. Charlotte Crutchfield’s (D-Montgomery) “Know Before They Knock” bill, which would require that police or social services workers provide oral and written notice to parents or caretakers of their rights if they are involved in an investigation of alleged child abuse or neglect. The bill failed to get out of committee in 2025 General Assembly.

The rally was joined by several lawmakers, including Sen. Shelly Hettleman (D-Baltimore County), Del. Gabriel Acevero (D-Montgomery) and Del. J. Sandy Bartlett (D-Anne Arundel), the new chair of the Judiciary Committee, who spoke in support of the public defenders. Others, like Del. N. Scott Phillips (D-Baltimore County), pressed for their own bills that are supported by the office.

Phillips, one of the first speakers at the rally, and Sen. Charles Sydnor III (D-Baltimore County) are both reintroducing bills this year that would reclassify some “non-safety related” offenses listed as secondary traffic offenses instead of primary violations, that would allow police to make a stop. Those include infractions like driving without an illuminated license plate, having excessive window tint or expired plates.

Drivers could still be cited for any of those violations, but only after being pulled over for another, primary violation.

Sydnor, who also attended Wednesday’s rally, presented his bill Tuesday during a nearly two-hour hearing of the Senate Judicial Proceedings Committee. He said this year’s version – Senate Bill 55 – would keep driving without a functioning headlight or taillights and driving in a bus-only lane as primary violations.

Sydnor emphasized that his bill seeks to not only reduce racial disparities in traffic stops but also protect officers.

“Categorizing non-safety related traffic stops that are disproportionately enforced on Black and brown Marylanders will enhance public safety by refocusing strained police resources on serious traffic offenses that threaten road safety and rebalancing police workload towards violent crime,” Sydnor said Tuesday.

“Through ongoing dialogue, we have significantly narrowed and altered this legislation from last year, and have struck a strong and smart balance with equity and safety concerns,” he said then.

The Governor’s Office of Crime Prevention and Policy’s traffic safety dashboard showed that in 2024, Blacks made up about 31% of the state’s population but ccounted for 42.4% of the 537,226 traffic stops that year. In comparison, whites made up almost 57% of the state’s population, but accounted for 38.1% of all traffic stops.

The dashboard also showed that while there were fewer traffic stops overall in 2023, at almost 483,000, the racial breakdown was essentially the same, with Blacks accounting for 43% of stops and whites making up 39.2%.

A polite, but firm, back-and-forth dialogue took place between Dartigue and Sen. William Folden (R-Frederick) at Tuesday’s hearing, when Dartigue reiterated how Black Marylanders are stopped more often than other drivers.

“I’ve heard of it from every person that came up, and I appreciate that,” said Folden, a recently retired police officer. “What I’m telling you is there’s other things that you are missing and it’s not about officer safety.

“It’s not even really necessarily about officer resources being applied elsewhere. It’s about stopping them from enforcing certain traffic laws that result in stops that potentially lead to other unfortunate arrests,” he said.

YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE.

“It would be a non-issue if everyone was stopped equally, but that is not what exists in Maryland,” Dartigue said.

The traffic-stop legislation got a boost Tuesday with testimony from Attorney General Anthony Brown (D) who offered several amendments, that include allowing a police officer to pull over a driver who commits more than one secondary violation and requiring that an officer inform a driver for all the reasons for a traffic stop.

“We think that we can achieve common ground, consensus around all these amendments to make [the bill] stronger,” he said.

No hearing dates have yet been set for Phillips’ version of the bill, which has been jointly assigned to the Judiciary and Environment and Transportation committees.
